newsitem.title: UK: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - U.S. ACQUISITIONS.
newsitem.headline: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - U.S. ACQUISITIONS.

text.p: THE PROTEUS COLUMN
Finding a bargain in the U.S. insurance acquisition market is becoming tougher and tougher.

In the last few months, buyers have paid top dollar for some of the big insurance companies that were up for sale as they moved to establish themselves as survivors in the rapidly changing U.S. market.
SAFECO Corp, often viewed as a cautious company, stunned observers in June when it agreed to pay Lincoln National Corp $2.8 billion for its American States Financial Corp property-casualty business.
A month later Lincoln National agreed to acquire the individual life insurance business of CIGNA Corp for $1.4 billion.
The American States property-casualty business sold at 16.7 times trailing twelve month earnings compared with an industry median of 10.3 in the first half of 1997 and 14.8 in 1996.
CIGNA's life business sold at 17.7 times trailing twelve month earnings compared with an industry median of 15.3 in the first half of 1997 and 14.3 in 1996.
The increase in the prices was confirmed last week in a report from U.S. research firm SNL Securities.
Prices are increasing as buyers scramble to snap up attractive properties in a bid to gain economies of scale and competitive advantages in an otherwise stagnant market.
And in what has become a game of musical chairs, the remaining good companies are the ones that command the higher prices, Schroder & Co analyst Andrew Kligerman noted.
But with deal prices at such high levels, the pool of potential buyers may begin to narrow.
Merrill Lynch analyst Jay Cohen sees the strongest buyers as those with large amounts of cash on their balance sheets or with access to cheap capital.
That leaves just a handful of companies in the United States and a group of big foreign companies on the list of potential buyers.
Cohen also sees the high prices leaving buyers little room for error after an acquisition is made. Such an environment may favour proven consolidators over newcomers to the merger market.
The high prices also may start to tempt more insurers to put themselves on the auction block.
That may keep deal prices from escalating further. But Cohen said buying interest is so high at the moment that he does not expect a decline in prices either.
